title: Lithvestor Review 2026: Is It Safe to Sign Up?
description: Lithvestor review for Australians: the AUD 400 minimum deposit, a 30% profit example, and what its site leaves out about licence and operator.
author: Sophia Reynolds
excerpt: Lithvestor review for Australians: the AUD 400 minimum deposit, a 30% profit example, and what its site leaves out about licence and operator.
content:
Lithvestor presents itself as an AI-powered trading platform for Australia that buys and sells cryptocurrencies across markets to build returns from small price differences. Its site promises stable profits and consistent returns from an entry deposit of AUD 400, and names no regulator and no operating company.

This review summarises what the Lithvestor site says about its method, costs, payments and support, points out what its pages leave out, and lists the checks Australian readers should run before they register.

Lithvestor Explained: What the Site Describes

According to its site, Lithvestor monitors several trading platforms for price differences, buys on one market and sells on another, and uses adaptable bots that apply AI strategies autonomously. You set the approach, risk level, markets and goals.

The home page names Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Litecoin and Dash first, then altcoins and stablecoins, and also lists forex, stocks, other securities, commodities and fractional shares. It describes itself as available globally while presenting itself as an Australian platform.

Platform Overview

Category Description
Platform Type AI-powered trading platform using arbitrage-style bots, per the site
Minimum Deposit AUD 400; the calculator runs from AUD 400 to AUD 16,000
Registration Fee None stated; the site says investors in Australia are never charged for using it
Payment Methods Credit cards, PayPal, bank transfer
Withdrawals Any time, per the FAQ; payouts within 24 to 48 hours
Support 24/7 listed, with a personal account manager; no channel or hours given
Mobile Access An app is mentioned ("Trade anytime, anywhere") with no download details
Security Claims SSL/TLS, bank-level encryption, two-factor authentication
Brokers "First-class brokers", none named
Operator No company name, address or registration number given

Everything in this table is what the site states. We have not tested any of it and could not confirm it independently.

Lithvestor: Where It Delivers, Where It Doesn’t

Fair reviews cut both ways. Here is what the site offers, and what does not add up.

Lithvestor strengths, per its site:

  • The minimum deposit is stated plainly as AUD 400, in Australian dollars.
  • Credit cards, PayPal and bank transfer are listed as ways to fund the account.
  • Withdrawals are described as available at any time, with payouts in 24 to 48 hours.
  • Two-factor authentication and SSL/TLS encryption are mentioned.
  • The terms say Australian law applies and set a minimum age of 18.

Where Lithvestor Falls Short:

  • No regulator, licence number, company name or address is named, although the FAQ calls the platform fully legal in Australia.
  • The site promises stable profits and consistent returns, and shows a 30% profit example over 45 days, with no risk warning on the page.
  • No trading, spread, broker or withdrawal fees are listed, only that platform access is free.
  • The brokers it works with are not named, and the terms say services may be managed by external providers.
  • Well-known exchange and media logos appear as trusted partners with no relationship explained.

A confident promise of stable profits is not a credential. Judge Lithvestor on what you can verify, not on the returns it shows.

What Actually Happens Behind Lithvestor

The site says software watches several platforms for price gaps and acts on them, and that AI bots run the strategy on their own once you set a risk level. It presents this as a way to build returns from small price changes.

A specialist or adviser then calls you after you submit the sign-up form, and the site mentions a personal account manager. The FAQ also says the platform manages your capital automatically and can produce returns without deep market knowledge.

None of this describes a method that can be checked, and a platform that promises returns without knowledge deserves extra care. Treat the automation as a claim, not as a feature we have confirmed.

Getting Set Up: What the Process Looks Like

This is the sign-up flow as the Lithvestor site describes it. We did not go through it ourselves.

1. Join

Fill in the Join Now form with your details. The site says a specialist or adviser will then call you.

2. Deposit funds

The minimum is AUD 400, paid by credit card, PayPal or bank transfer. The calculator on the site goes up to AUD 16,000.

3. Let the bots trade

Choose the approach, risk level, markets and goals, and the bots trade autonomously. The FAQ says you can add funds or withdraw at any time.

Expect a phone call after you register. You are never obliged to deposit because someone on the phone suggests a bigger amount.

Breaking Down What Lithvestor Costs

The site says all fees are transparent and that it never charges investors in Australia for using the platform. Access is described as free from Australia.

No schedule of trading, spread, broker or withdrawal fees is shown, and the terms do not mention fees. Before you deposit, look for:

  • The spread or commission on each trade, and who charges it.
  • Withdrawal fees and the minimum withdrawal amount.
  • Currency conversion charges if your deposit is not in Australian dollars.
  • Any fee a broker or external provider adds on top.

The calculator on the home page shows a 30% profit over 45 days on AUD 400. It is an illustration, not a projection, and it comes with no explanation of how it was calculated.

Which Assets Lithvestor Covers

The site lists Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Litecoin and Dash by name, plus altcoins and stablecoins, and says it also covers forex, stocks, other securities, commodities and fractional shares. The FAQ ends its list with the words and more.

We could not confirm which of these you can actually trade, or through which broker. Check inside your account before you rely on it:

  • Which assets and pairs are really available, and whether stocks and forex are offered to retail clients in your country.
  • The name and licence of the broker or exchange that executes the trades.
  • Whether spreads and charges differ by asset.

Is Lithvestor Legit in Australia?

The FAQ calls Lithvestor a fully legal and reliable trading platform in Australia and says it is not a scam or fraud. It names no regulator, licence or registration number, and the generic line about complying with applicable regulations is the only compliance statement.

Points that do not add up:

  • No company, address or registration number appears on the home page, the About page or the terms; only a copyright line.
  • The terms say Australian law applies, but do not say which Australian entity is bound by them.
  • The terms say services may be managed by external providers, and the site does not name the brokers it works with.
  • Fees are called transparent, yet none are listed beyond platform access.
  • Stable profits and a 30% example are shown, while the terms put all risk on the user and contain no trading risk disclosure.

In Australia, businesses offering financial products or services to retail clients generally need an Australian Financial Services licence from ASIC. We could not confirm that Lithvestor holds one. Checks you can run yourself:

  • Search the company name and any licence number on ASIC’s Financial Services Register.
  • Check ASIC’s investor alert list for the name and the website address.
  • Search the name on Scamwatch and MoneySmart for scam reports.
  • Ask for the legal entity name and licence number in writing before you deposit.
  • Check whether the firm belongs to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA).
  • Look up when the domain was registered, since a very new domain deserves extra care.

Legitimacy and profitability are different things. Even a licensed platform can lose you money if you overcommit or rely on best-case figures. This section is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Mistakes Worth Avoiding on Lithvestor

Most of the losses with automated trading tools trace back to user decisions, not the platform itself. A few worth flagging:

Assuming the name means the platform is established.

A memorable brand is not a substitute for checking the platform’s actual history and terms.

Funding well beyond the minimum right away.

Test the platform on your own terms before scaling up. That is exactly why a small first deposit makes sense.

Treating AI-assisted trading as fully hands-off.

Check your open positions regularly. Market conditions shift, and settings that worked last month may not fit now.

Ignoring fees and spreads.

Small per-trade costs add up once you make a reasonable number of trades. Read the current terms first.

Skipping a small test withdrawal.

Payout terms are easy to overlook until you need them. Try a small withdrawal while the amount is still low.

A Quick Checklist Before Your First Live Trade

Run through this before committing real funds.

  • Company name and licence number obtained and checked on ASIC’s register.
  • Fees, spreads and withdrawal charges confirmed in writing.
  • The brokers named, and their licences checked.
  • Adviser calls treated as sales calls, with no deposit made during the call.
  • First deposit kept to the AUD 400 minimum or less than you can afford to lose.
  • A small withdrawal tested early, before depositing more.
  • Stable profit and 30% claims treated as marketing until a method is shown.

Who Gets the Most Out of Lithvestor

Lithvestor may suit a newcomer who wants a low entry point of AUD 400, will read the terms first and is prepared to verify the operator and its brokers independently before depositing.

It is a poor fit for anyone who needs a named regulator and operator, who plans to rely on stable profit claims, or who wants an income they can leave on autopilot.

The platform underneath the claims is unconfirmed. Judge it on what you can check, not on the branding.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Lithvestor legit?

We could not confirm it. The site calls itself legal in Australia but names no regulator, licence or operating company, so check ASIC’s Financial Services Register before you deposit.

Is Lithvestor a scam?

We cannot say either way. The site promises stable profits, names no operator and does not name its brokers, so start small, test a withdrawal early and register only through the official website.

Is Lithvestor legit in Australia?

The site is aimed at Australia and says Australian law applies, but it gives no Australian entity or AFS licence number. Check ASIC’s register and investor alert list first.

What is the Lithvestor minimum deposit?

AUD 400, according to the site. Its calculator runs from AUD 400 to AUD 16,000.

Does Lithvestor charge fees?

The site says access is free for investors in Australia and that fees are transparent, but it lists no trading, spread, broker or withdrawal fees.

How long does a Lithvestor withdrawal take?

The FAQ says payouts are processed within 24 to 48 hours and that you can withdraw at any time. It does not describe fees, limits or verification steps.

Does Lithvestor have a mobile app?

The site mentions an app and the line trade anytime, anywhere, but gives no download details. Use only the official website and be careful of look-alike apps.

What payment methods does Lithvestor accept?

Credit cards, PayPal and bank transfer are listed on the site.

Who is behind Lithvestor?

The site names no legal entity, address or registration number. The About page lists a team with job titles, which we could not verify.

Does Lithvestor guarantee profits?

The site speaks of stable profits and consistent returns, but no return is guaranteed. Treat the 30% example and the testimonials as marketing.

Where We Land on Lithvestor

Lithvestor offers a familiar AI-assisted pitch with a stated AUD 400 entry point and free access for Australian investors, according to its own site. What it does not offer is a named regulator, a named operating company or a named broker.

If you decide to try it, keep the first deposit small, confirm the licence on ASIC’s register, and test a withdrawal before you add funds.
